facts.statement: Nichollssaura was an extinct genus of leptocleidid plesiosaur that lived in the Early Cretaceous Boreal Sea of North America.
facts.quote: Nichollssaura is an extinct genus of leptocleidid plesiosaur from the Early Cretaceous Boreal Sea of North America.

facts.statement: Nichollssaura was a small plesiosaur estimated to reach 2.6 to 2.9 meters in length and 135 kilograms in body mass.
facts.quote: Nichollssaura was a small plesiosaur, estimated up to 2.6 - 2.9 m in length and 135 kg in body mass based on a complete specimen (TMP 1994.122.1).

facts.statement: The holotype specimen preserves most of the skeleton, though it is missing the left forelimb and scapula, parts of the right hindlimb, and several ribs on the left side.
facts.quote: Most of the skeleton is preserved, missing only the left forelimb and scapula, the bones distal to the ankle on the right hindlimb, and the proximal third of the cervical ribs on the left side, and the first few anterior dorsal ribs, also on the left side.

facts.statement: The type specimen was discovered in 1994 in an open-pit oil sands mine near Fort McMurray, Alberta, within the Wabiskaw member of the Clearwater Formation.
facts.quote: The type specimen was discovered in one of Syncrude Canada Ltd.'s open-pit oilsand mines near Fort McMurray, Alberta, in 1994, in the Wabiskaw member of the Clearwater Formation.

facts.statement: Parts of the holotype skeleton were accidentally lost when 100-ton electric shovel operators discovered the fossil.
facts.quote: These were lost when the specimen was discovered accidentally by 100-ton electric shovel operators Greg Fisher and Lorne Cundal.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen contained 165 gastroliths made of chert and quartzite, with the largest stone weighing an estimated 9.96 grams.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen preserves 165 gastroliths composed of cherts and quartzites, the largest of which had an estimated weight of 9.96 grams.

facts.statement: Researchers hypothesize that Nichollssaura swam westward to collect gastroliths from rocks that were 8 to 10 million years older than the animal itself.
facts.quote: These rocks are 8-10 million years older than the Wabiskaw member plesiosaurs, so it is hypothesized that they may have swum westward from the northern Western Interior Seaway to collect the Cadomin rocks eroding out of the beaches and river mouths of the Seaway's western coast.

facts.statement: The genus Nichollssaura was described by Druckenmiller and Russell in 2009.
The genus was originally named Nichollsia in honor of curator Dr. Betsy Nicholls but had to be renamed because that name was already taken by a genus of isopods.
facts.quote: The fossil, named after paleontological curator Dr. Betsy Nicholls, originally was named Nichollsia borealis but Nichollsia was already in use (preoccupied) by a genus of isopods.

facts.statement: The type species N. borealis lived during the early Albian age in what is now Alberta, Canada.
facts.quote: The type species is N. borealis, found in the early Albian age Clearwater Formation near Fort McMurray, Alberta, Canada.

facts.statement: Nichollssaura lived between 113.2 and 100.5 million years ago during the Albian stage.
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Albian (113.2 to 100.5 million years ago)

facts.statement: Nichollssaura is classified within the family Leptocleididae.

rejected.statement: Nichollssaura fills an approximate 40-million-year gap in the fossil record of North American plesiosaurs.
rejected.quote: It fills an approximate 40-million-year gap in the fossil record of North American plesiosaurs.
